elements.text:
I took a bit of a detour today on additional sha vectorizations. I added the vectorization of endianness conversions and or k-adding. I recently moved k-adding to its own function with additions enumerated across the buffer, but there was a bug in the vectorization. I tracked that down today and was able to enable this and the vectorized endianness conversions.

These save approximately a total of 5% for smaller hashing runs, declining as the size of the buffer increases. They also save 1-3% of Merkle hashing runs, again with the primary benefit on the low end (this makes sense as they only affect the 1/2/3 lane merkle hashes (unvectorized)).

elements.text: We are able to take advantage of several vectorizations that Core and typical hash libraries cannot, because we use buffered scheduling of the message, as opposed to variable rotation.  This uses more memory, but allows significant net time savings through vectorization. The sha256 buffer is 4x the 64 byte block size, rotating. So that's not really significant. So we vectorize across the message buffer: sigma computations, endianness conversion, and k-addition but also vectorize across multiple message buffers (the other axis), and finally vectorize across independent hashes for Merkle (which Core does as well).

elements.text: Notice also that performance in the first 100k blocks doesn't really make a difference in overall performance, as long as there are at at least 8 threads. Completion rapidly converges around block 400. So 8 threads would be sufficient, but we want to get started as fast as possible as well. So for this 8 dual core machine on a 2.3Gbps network, we want at least 32 logical threads, which is twice the number of physical threads. elements.text: block.prepopulate()
obtains all previous outputs of tx inputs within the block that are present within the block and attaches them to the
.prevout
metadata field of spending input. Later when the
query.populate(block)

is called these prevouts are skipped. This saves database search and deserialization for some number of prevouts (I will trace that value per block, it would be interesting to know). The downside is that the iteration within the block is repeated. This turns out to be a worthwhile tradeoff, as the prepopulating run is 9.7 minutes faster, or 97.5% of the no-populate run. There is very little variation across runs since this is independent of the network. So while this is a small optimization, it is one line of code that turns out to be worthwhile. I'll disable the configuration option as there is no reason to disable the behavior now that it is verified.
